name: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm
aliases: intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm of the pancreas

reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A mucin-producing epithelial neoplasm arising within the pancreatic ducts, classified as main-duct, branch-duct, or mixed type
Main-duct and mixed types carry a substantially higher risk of high-grade dysplasia and invasive carcinoma than branch-duct disease
Branch-duct lesions communicate with the main duct and are frequently multifocal, often found incidentally as cystic lesions
A classic endoscopic finding of main-duct disease is a patulous, mucin-extruding ampulla (the fish-mouth papilla)
Worrisome features and high-risk stigmata (as in the international consensus and European guidelines) drive decisions between surveillance and resection
High-risk stigmata include obstructive jaundice with a pancreatic head cyst, an enhancing mural nodule of significant size, and marked main pancreatic duct dilatation
Worrisome features include cyst growth, thickened enhancing cyst walls, smaller mural nodules, an abrupt duct calibre change with distal atrophy, and raised CA 19-9
Management ranges from periodic imaging surveillance for low-risk branch-duct lesions to surgical resection for main-duct disease and lesions with high-risk features
reference.pathophysiology: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms are proliferations of mucin-secreting columnar epithelium that grow within and dilate the pancreatic ductal system. Excess mucin production and papillary epithelial growth obstruct the ducts, producing cystic dilatation of branch ducts, diffuse or segmental dilatation of the main duct, or both. These lesions progress through a spectrum from low-grade dysplasia to high-grade dysplasia and, ultimately, invasive adenocarcinoma, following an adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence. The malignant potential correlates with the ductal compartment involved and with morphological features such as mural nodules, main duct dilatation, and epithelial subtype, with pancreatobiliary and intestinal subtypes behaving differently.
additionalDifferentials: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas
Chronic obstructive pancreatitis with duct dilatation
additionalInvestigations: MRI with MRCP to assess ductal communication, cyst morphology, and main duct calibre
Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration for cyst fluid and mural nodule assessment
Cyst fluid CEA (elevated in mucinous lesions) and cytology
Cyst fluid molecular analysis for KRAS and GNAS mutations to support the diagnosis
Serum CA 19-9 as a marker of concern for malignancy
Contrast-enhanced CT to evaluate for a solid mass or vascular involvement
ERCP or pancreatoscopy in selected cases to inspect the duct directly
redFlags: Obstructive jaundice attributable to a cystic head lesion
An enhancing mural nodule of significant size or a solid component
Marked dilatation of the main pancreatic duct
New-onset diabetes, weight loss, or rapid cyst growth
Positive or high-grade atypical cytology on aspiration
reference.prognosis: Branch-duct lesions without worrisome features generally have a low short-term risk of malignancy and can be safely surveyed, whereas main-duct and mixed lesions carry a high risk of harbouring or progressing to invasive cancer; outcomes after resection depend on whether invasive carcinoma is present and on its stage and subtype.
pitfalls: Misclassifying a mucinous cyst as a benign serous cystadenoma or pseudocyst
Under-recognising main-duct involvement and its high malignant potential
Discontinuing surveillance prematurely, as risk persists and can increase over time
Attributing main duct dilatation to chronic pancreatitis and missing an IPMN
Over-reliance on cyst size alone rather than the full set of worrisome and high-risk features
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
International (Fukuoka/Kyoto) consensus guidelines on IPMN of the pancreas
European evidence-based guidelines on pancreatic cystic neoplasms
management: Stratify risk using worrisome features and high-risk stigmata to decide between surveillance and resection
Surveil branch-duct lesions without worrisome features with serial MRI/MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound
Resect main-duct, mixed-type and high-risk lesions surgically by pancreaticoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy given their malignant potential
Characterise indeterminate lesions with endoscopic ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration for cyst fluid analysis and mural nodule assessment
Manage post-resection exocrine and endocrine insufficiency with pancreatic enzyme replacement and insulin
Continue long-term surveillance of the pancreatic remnant after resection given the field defect and risk of new lesions
Refer to a hepatobiliary and pancreatic multidisciplinary team for management decisions
